Ocean tides are driven mainly by the Moon's gravitational pull, which is stronger on the side of Earth facing it and weaker on the far side, stretching the ocean into two bulges. Earth rotates through those bulges, so most coasts see two high and two low tides a day. The Sun adds a weaker pull that reinforces the Moon's at new and full moon (spring tides) and partly cancels it at the quarter moons (neap tides), while local coastline and seafloor shape set the actual range.

Tides come from the difference in gravitational pull across the Earth: the Moon tugs the near side more strongly than the planet's center and the center more strongly than the far side, stretching the oceans into two bulges on opposite sides. As the Earth rotates beneath those bulges, most coastlines pass through two highs and two lows roughly every 24 hours and 50 minutes. The Sun adds a weaker pull of about half the Moon's tidal strength, so tides run large (spring) when Sun and Moon align at new and full moon, and small (neap) when they pull at right angles — with local coastline shape and basin resonance setting the actual range at any given place.
